Reviewing the Nanoscale Eyes: TEM vs. SEM

Since it has been a while, let’s start with a quick warm-up. We previously discussed two major acronyms in the world of microscopy: TEM and SEM.

TEM stands for Transmission Electron Microscope. As the name suggests, you prepare your specimen as an incredibly thin slice—so thin that the electron beam can actually transmit all the way through it to hit a sensor or screen at the bottom. Because the beam passes through the sample, the resulting image is based on contrast; some areas are more opaque to the electrons, while others are more transparent.

SEM stands for Scanning Electron Microscope. Instead of shooting electrons through the sample, the SEM scans a beam across the surface and measures the electrons that are absorbed or reflected (backscattered) off the topography.

TEM is fantastic for imaging incredibly tiny biological entities. People routinely use it to look at viruses, strands of DNA, or even individual atoms. You get what you pay for—it offers staggering resolution. However, there are significant downsides. The equipment is expensive, and sample preparation is a massive pain. For a standard TEM, your biological samples usually have to be dead, often frozen, and sliced painstakingly thin.

The SEM, on the other hand, is much easier to use. You do not have to slice your samples into atomic-scale deli meats. You can look at the detailed 3D surface structures of things like pollen grains or the antennae of an ant. There are even variants of SEMs that operate with water vapor and warmer temperatures, allowing you to image living organisms!

By the way, did you know you can actually get trained to use an SEM right here on campus? Through a program called Nano Train—spearheaded by our upcoming guest lecturer, Prof. Marc Michel—you can get hands-on training and earn one credit of Nano 4994. It is a fantastic resume builder. When you tell a prospective faculty supervisor that you already know how to operate an SEM, they will be thrilled to have you in their lab.

Building at the Nanoscale: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up

Now, let’s talk about how we actually make nanoscale objects. Earlier in the semester, we discussed photolithography, which is how we pattern semiconductors and transistors for microchips. Lithography is a top-down process. You start with a large bulk piece of material and chisel it down, step by step, into smaller and smaller patterns.

But there is an alternative approach: the bottom-up process. Instead of chiseling down a block of marble, why not start with the smallest possible building blocks—individual atoms or molecules—and have them come together to form ordered nanoscale structures?

If you think about it, this is exactly how nature operates. We, as human beings, are bottom-up fabricated objects. Nobody took a giant chunk of carbon-based material and chiseled it into the shape of a person. We started from tiny cellular and molecular components that assembled themselves into a complex organism.

Moving Atoms One by One (The Hard Way)

Humanity has actually pushed this bottom-up concept to its absolute limit. For a few decades now, we have possessed the technology to physically push and move individual atoms around to form whatever shapes we want.

This is done using an instrument called a Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM). Unlike the electron microscopes we just discussed, an STM uses an incredibly sharp tip that parks just above the surface of a specimen. By measuring the quantum tunneling current of electrons jumping between the tip and the sample, we can map out individual atoms. If we tune the electrical and mechanical parameters just right, we can actually use that tip to drag atoms across the surface.

To prove just how precise this technology is, researchers at IBM used an STM to create a stop-motion cartoon called A Boy and His Atom. They used the STM tip to manually drag individual carbon monoxide molecules across a copper crystal surface, taking an image after every tiny movement to create the frames of the animation.

It is an astonishing technical achievement, but as you might imagine, it is not exactly practical for mass manufacturing.

To make this work, the entire system had to be kept in an ultra-clean vacuum and cooled to an extremely low temperature—around 4 Kelvin, just single digits above absolute zero! If you tried to do this at room temperature in normal air, the atoms would be jiggling all over the place due to thermal energy, and the surface would be covered in atmospheric junk. Furthermore, dragging one atom at a time is agonizingly slow. If our goal is to manufacture millions of commercial memory devices or nanoscale drug carriers, moving atoms one by one is simply not the way to go.

Self-Assembly and the Magic of Surfactants

Instead of forcing atoms into place, it would be far preferable if we could get molecules to assemble themselves on their own. Think of the liquid metal Terminator from Terminator 2, pulling its scattered pieces back together into a cohesive form. We want to design molecular building blocks that naturally organize into useful nanoscale structures.

The classic building blocks for self-assembly are a class of molecules called surfactants. You can think of a surfactant molecule as looking a bit like a tadpole, consisting of two distinct parts with opposing personalities.

The "head" of the molecule is polar and hydrophilic. The suffix -philic means "loving" (just like Philadelphia is the city of brotherly love). This part of the molecule loves water and wants to interact with it.

The "tail" of the molecule is a hydrocarbon chain that is hydrophobic. The suffix -phobic means "fearing" or "hating" (like arachnophobia is the fear of spiders). This part of the molecule strongly repels water.

Micelles, Bilayers, and Washing Your Hands

You actually take advantage of surfactant self-assembly every single day. I hope everyone is using soap when they wash their hands! The active ingredient in many soaps is a surfactant called sodium stearate.

When you wash your hands, the dirt and oils on your skin are hydrophobic (they do not mix with water). The soap molecules rush in, and their water-hating hydrocarbon tails eagerly bury themselves into the oil and grime to escape the water. Meanwhile, the water-loving polar heads face outward toward the aqueous environment of your sink. They naturally arrange themselves into a little spherical cage around the dirt, called a micelle. Once the dirt is trapped inside this water-soluble sphere, it washes easily down the drain.

Depending on the concentration of the surfactants and their specific geometry, they do not always form little spheres. Sometimes, they self-assemble into a flat sheet called a bilayer. In a bilayer, two layers of surfactant molecules line up tail-to-tail. The hydrophobic tails hide in the interior of the sandwich, completely shut off from the water, while the hydrophilic heads face outward on both sides.

Liposomes: Nature’s Tiny Delivery Vehicles

If you have a flat sheet of this lipid bilayer floating in water, you run into a geometric problem. The molecules in the middle of the sheet are happy, but what about the edges? At the perimeter of the sheet, the hydrophobic tails are exposed directly to the water. Those molecules are not happy at all.

To resolve this tension, the bilayer sheet will naturally curve and fold in on itself. By curling up into a closed, continuous pouch, it eliminates the exposed edges entirely. All the hydrophobic tails are now safely hidden inside the walls of the pouch. We call this self-assembled hollow sphere a liposome (or a vesicle).

Liposomes are absolute superstars in the field of nanomedicine. They act as tiny, customizable drug carriers, typically ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers in diameter.

Because a liposome is a hollow pouch made of a bilayer, it has two distinct storage compartments. The interior core of the pouch is filled with water, making it a great place to store hydrophilic drug molecules. Alternatively, if you are trying to deliver a hydrophobic drug that hates water, you can embed those drug molecules directly inside the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer wall itself.

To make these carriers even smarter, researchers can functionalize the outside of the liposome. This means attaching specific molecules to the outer surface that act like homing beacons or molecular Velcro. When you inject these functionalized liposomes into a patient’s bloodstream, they ignore healthy tissue and only bind to specific targets, like cancer cells.

Once the liposome binds to the cancer cell and gets absorbed inside, we face one final challenge: the drug is still trapped inside the pouch! We have to pop it. As you may recall from our previous guest lecture, one way to do this is using focused ultrasound. By targeting ultrasound waves at the tumor site, we can locally heat the liposomes to about 40 degrees Celsius (roughly the temperature of a high fever). This gentle, localized heating destabilizes the liposome, causing it to burst and release the drug exactly where it is needed, without overwhelming the rest of the patient’s body.

Expanding the Arsenal: Other Nanoparticles

While liposomes are brilliant, they are just one type of self-assembled nanostructure. Depending on the chemistry we use, we can engineer a variety of different nanoparticles for medical applications. For instance, we can create solid polymer-based nanoparticles, or core-shell nanoshells that feature an inorganic core (like silica or iron oxide) wrapped in a metal coating (like gold or silver).

To see just how sophisticated these designs can get, we can look at the work of Prof. Paula Hammond at MIT. She and her team engineered a multi-layered "superweapon" nanoparticle to fight highly aggressive, drug-resistant forms of cancer.

Some cancer cells are incredibly stubborn; they actually pump chemotherapy drugs out of their systems before the poison can kill them. To defeat this, Prof. Hammond’s team built a nanoparticle with several distinct layers:

  1. The Core: A capsule containing the actual chemotherapy drug.

  2. The Inner Shell: A layer of siRNA (short genetic sequences). These act as gene blockers. When released inside the cell, they turn off the cancer cell’s specific survival genes, disabling its ability to pump out the chemotherapy drug.

  3. The Protective Layer: Because siRNA is negatively charged, it is wrapped in a positively charged polymer to hold it all together.

  4. The Outer Cloak: A highly hydrated, negatively charged polysaccharide layer. This acts as an invisibility cloak, hiding the nanoparticle from the body’s immune system so it is not destroyed while traveling through the bloodstream. This outer layer also contains the targeting molecules that bind specifically to the tumor.

When tested on mice with aggressive tumors, the results were astounding. Mice treated with just the chemotherapy drug saw their tumors continue to grow rapidly. But mice treated with the multi-layered superweapon saw their tumors stop growing, shrink, and in some cases, disappear entirely.

To wrap up today’s concepts, I want to leave you with a quick thought experiment. We saw earlier that when you put surfactants in water, they form a micelle with the hydrophilic heads facing outward and the hydrophobic tails hiding on the inside.

What do you think would happen if you took those exact same surfactant molecules and dropped them into a vat of oil instead of water?

Because oil is a hydrocarbon, the environment is reversed. The hydrophobic tails actually love the oil, while the hydrophilic heads hate it! As a result, the molecules self-assemble inside-out. The water-loving heads cluster together in the center to hide, and the tails point outward into the oil. We call this structure an inverse micelle. It is a beautiful demonstration of how the rules of self-assembly adapt to their environment.
